chunks: Ali ibn al-Hasan narrated from Muhammad ibn Khalid from Saif ibn 'Amirah from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) who said:

I said to him: A man divorced his wife, then took her back in the presence of witnesses, then divorced her again, then changed his mind and took her back in the presence of witnesses, then divorced her again, then took her back in the presence of witnesses. Is she completely divorced from him? He said: 'Yes.' I said: All of that was in one period of purity? He said: 'She is completely divorced from him.' I said: If he did that with a pregnant woman, is she completely divorced from him? He said: 'This is not like that.'

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: The meaning in this report is that if he divorces her three times in one period of purity according to the Sunnah, then she is completely divorced from him by the three, as we have mentioned, even if he had not consummated the marriage with her, because every time he takes her back, it is permissible for him to divorce her another time according to the Sunnah, as we have mentioned. And this is not found in the pregnant woman, because when he takes the pregnant woman back, it is not permissible for him to divorce her another time according to the Sunnah, as we have mentioned, until she gives birth to what is in her womb. And it is only permissible for him to divorce her for the waiting period if he has intercourse with her after the taking back, as we mentioned and detailed earlier.
ai.seo_question: Does triple divorce in one period of purity apply to pregnant women?
ai.summary: In this narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS), the distinction is drawn between a non-pregnant woman and a pregnant woman regarding the efficacy of triple divorce pronounced in a single period of purity. For the pregnant woman, the third divorce does not immediately sever the bond because the waiting period (iddah) is tied to childbirth rather than menstrual cycles, preventing the immediate application of the 'three divorces' rule until she delivers. This highlights the Shia jurisprudential nuance that the structural integrity of the marriage contract remains intact during the pregnancy period, altering the standard mechanics of talaq.
